newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Russia palladium supply woes roil market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia palladium supply woes roil market.

text.p: A protracted halt to Russian exports has thrown Japan's palladium market into turmoil, with traders scrambling for supplies while prices and lease rates surge, market sources said on Thursday.

With suppliers, end-users and local Japanese investors all likely to end up as losers in the current confusion, they added that the last laugh will probably be had by overseas speculative funds that took long positions when it became apparent Russia's shipments to Japan could face a long delay.
Russia's former Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin sought to calm the palladium market on Thursday. He told Reuters in Tokyo that there was no reason for panic in the world palladium market.

But in London on Thursday, palladium prices fixed at a fresh 21-month high of $160.25 an ounce, up $3.25 from the day before. Traders said palladium prices would rise further unless Russia resumes its exports.
Traders added that robust palladium demand for automotive catalysts in the U.S. and Europe would prevent palladium prices from falling even if Russia began exporting again.
As spot supplies grow increasingly tight, Japanese traders have been left scrambling to secure the metal they need.
"We are really at a loss what to do," an official at a major Japanese bullion house said. "We will have to struggle for a while to get metal in a panic-stricken market."
"We haven't covered our requirements for May yet, as we had been quite optimistic that Russia would resume metal sales in April," he said.
Annual Japan-Russia palladium supply talks, usually held in mid-December, have been postponed due to domestic developments in Russia.

The market suffered an additional shock earlier this week when a Russian trade official said there would be no palladium shipments to Japan in April and possibly none in May. It was not known when talks with Japan might be held.

Traders said that over the long term the delays were bound to be damaging to Russia, the world's largest palladium producer, as users in Japan, the world's biggest consumer, are increasingly switching to other metals due to high prices and supply uncertainty.
"A drop in Japan's palladium demand would be unavoidable as every palladium end-user in Japan is beginning to mull ways to avoid using palladium," a trading house trader said.

Market sources said electronics manufacturers, which account for about 60 percent of Japan's palladium demand, would switch to nickel and other cheaper metals at prices above 550 yen per gram. Yen-based palladium prices in the spot Tokyo market were quoted at about 660 yen on Thursday.

Traders also said that Japanese private investors, who accumulated massive short positions in yen-based TOCOM palladium futures on the belief that prices would tumble when Russia resumed shipments, appear likely to get fleeced during the current rally.
"Overseas funds are aiming to squeeze TOCOM's large short positions," a trader at a major trading house said.
"When private investors start covering their shorts, palladium prices could climb to $180 per ounce. A high of $200 per ounce may be within reach unless Russia resumes metal sales," he said.
Several traders said that the yen's recent tumble against the dollar also put Japanese private investors in a disadvantageous position.
The tightness in spot palladium supplies was also evident in the leasing market, where traders often borrow metal to cover short-term needs.
Short-term lease rates soared to 15 percent to 16 percent on Thursday, compared with about six percent on Tuesday and three percent earlier this year.
--Tokyo Commodity Desk, +81-3-3432-7431
